title: Boeing Wins $20B+ F/A-XX Carrier Fighter as Pentagon Hands Raytheon $20.7B to Double AMRAAM Output
subhead: The US Navy finally picks Boeing for its sixth-generation carrier fighter after more than a year of delays, while a record AMRAAM multiyear buy aims to refill air-to-air stocks drawn down by the Iran war — two awards that together define the Pentagon's push to rebuild capacity for high-end air combat.

sections.heading: Boeing Beats Northrop for F/A-XX, Ending a Year of Program Limbo
sections.body:
The US Navy has selected Boeing over Northrop Grumman to build its next-generation carrier-based stealth fighter, F/A-XX, according to Breaking Defense, The War Zone and Anadolu Agency. Anadolu put the contract value at more than $20 billion. Lockheed Martin had reportedly been eliminated from the running back in March 2025.

The decision closes a long stretch of uncertainty. The Pentagon moved to freeze F/A-XX in June 2025, arguing the US industrial base could not support two sixth-generation fighter programs at once — Boeing had already won the Air Force's F-47 competition three months earlier. Congress intervened to keep F/A-XX alive, and in April 2026 Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle said a winner would be named by August. That deadline slipped, and as recently as last month Caudle told Aviation Week he no longer knew when a decision would come.

Boeing's win is unsurprising given that context: The War Zone notes the company can leverage design work and supply chains already developed for the F-47, and had publicly disputed claims it could not meet Air Force and Navy needs simultaneously. Industrial-base skepticism had not fully disappeared — Air Force Gen. Dale White reiterated capacity concerns about building both aircraft just two weeks ago.
sections.whyItMatters: The US Navy now has a shipboard sixth-generation fighter program with a builder, after nearly two years of near-cancellation. It also concentrates two next-generation US fighter programs in one company, deepening dependence on Boeing's defense division even as questions about its capacity to deliver both remain open.

sections.heading: Raytheon's $20.7B AMRAAM Deal Aims to Nearly Double Missile Output
sections.body:
The Pentagon awarded RTX's Raytheon a multiyear contract worth up to $20.7 billion to build Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missiles (AMRAAMs), Defense News reports — a ceiling that dwarfs the previous record $3.5 billion AMRAAM award from July 2025. The department said the five-year deal, with two option years, will nearly double AMRAAM production and is a joint buy by the Air Force, the Navy and allies.

The award was made Sept. 25 and announced Monday under the Pentagon's Arsenal of Freedom campaign to expand weapons output. RTX has committed under earlier framework agreements to raise annual output to at least 1,900 AMRAAMs, more than 1,000 Tomahawks and 500-plus Standard Missile-6 interceptors. Reuters reported the AMRAAM award is provisional — Congress has not yet funded the full deal, and executives have warned contractors may hold off on factory and parts investment until lawmakers act.

RTX says AMRAAM is fielded by 44 countries and is the primary interceptor for NASAMS, the ground-based air-defense system that guards Washington and is used by more than a dozen nations. The Pentagon is already preparing a successor: earlier this month it signed a framework deal with Lockheed Martin to boost production of the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the clearest signal yet of how much air-to-air stock the US and its allies burned through in the Iran war. The multiyear authority is designed to give industry the demand certainty to invest — but the funding gap means the production ramp is not yet real.

sections.heading: Israel Signs Its Largest-Ever Arms Deal: a €3B 'Achilles Shield' for Greece
sections.body:
Israel and Greece signed a defense export agreement worth roughly €3 billion ($3.5 billion) under which Israel will build Greece a multi-layered air-defense array combining several Israeli systems — dubbed the Achilles Shield. AP, Politico Europe and defence-blog reported the deal, which both sides describe as their largest to date. Politico notes Greece will be the first country to acquire so broad a package: Germany bought Arrow 3 in 2023 and Finland acquired David's Sling in 2024, but Athens is going further.

The deal has already stirred controversy. Anadolu Agency reports that Greece's opposition is demanding clarity after an Israeli official said source code was not included in the $3.5 billion user license — raising questions about how much operational control Athens actually gains over the system. A September report by the Turkish think tank ORSAM, cited by Nordic Monitor, argues the shield could materially expand Greece's ability to detect and intercept targets, shifting the Aegean military balance.
sections.whyItMatters: Israel converts its wartime air-defense expertise into its biggest export contract, embedding itself deep in a European NATO member's air-defense architecture. For Greece it is a hedge against Turkey; for Israel it is a strategic and commercial foothold in Europe — with the source-code dispute showing the limits of what buyers actually get.

sections.heading: Japan Opens Its Arms Market With the Biggest Export Rule Change in Decades
sections.body:
Japan has overhauled its defense export rules, opening the door to global arms sales in what Reuters framed as the biggest such change in decades. The shift builds on Tokyo's April 2026 revision of the Three Principles on Transfer of Defense Equipment and Technology, which lifted a ban on lethal weapons exports. NHK and CSIS have tracked the policy turn as a deliberate effort to strengthen Japan's defense industrial base and deepen ties with security partners.

The move is drawing international attention. Reuters reported that US allies rattled by Trump-era pressure on security guarantees are eyeing Japan's opening, and Japan is considering missile exports to the Philippines. The Straits Times reported separately that Japan may raise defense spending toward 3.5% of GDP after US pressure. China's state media has attacked the policy as a 'neo-militarist' turn.
sections.whyItMatters: Japan is moving from self-imposed restraint to active arms exporter, potentially becoming a new supplier for Indo-Pacific partners — notably the Philippines. Combined with spending possibly heading toward 3.5% of GDP, this is the most significant change to Japan's postwar defense posture in years.

sections.heading: US Stores Typhon Missile System at Kadena as Okinawa Burden Grows
sections.body:
Japan's Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said the US Typhon missile system — capable of firing Tomahawk cruise missiles — will be transferred from Kanoya Air Base in Kagoshima to US Kadena Air Base in Okinawa around mid-October, along with HIMARS launchers, Kyodo reported via Japan Today. Koizumi said the systems would not be stored permanently and no unit would be stationed to operate them.

The Typhon deployment has drawn criticism from China and Russia. Local anger is also rising: Kadena Mayor Hiroshi Toyama protested to the Defense Ministry on Monday, calling the plan 'totally unacceptable' and saying it ignored residents' feelings about the base-hosting burden on Okinawa.
sections.whyItMatters: Relocating Typhon to Okinawa keeps a Tomahawk-capable system in the first island chain while Beijing and Moscow watch closely. Tokyo is trying to signal deterrence without permanently basing the system — a balancing act that satisfies neither local residents nor regional critics.

sections.heading: NATO's Nuclear Posture Tightens Around a Nervous Eastern Flank
sections.body:
NATO is working on plans to expand its nuclear deterrent in Europe in response to Russian threats, according to research by the German Press Agency reported by Anadolu Agency, including discussion of additional US nuclear deployments. The debate is intensifying on the alliance's eastern edge: Lithuania's parliament advanced a proposal to lift its constitutional ban on weapons of mass destruction, with backers arguing that 'Russians do not attack the strong,' per EUobserver and The Defense Post. The Kremlin warned that lifting the ban would bring 'great danger' to Lithuania rather than security, Izvestia reported.

Separately, experts cited by Euronews argue that the alliance's failure to respond forcefully to Russian hybrid attacks is eroding deterrence, while analysts quoted on the Yasen-M submarine threat warn of a growing undersea challenge across the GIUK Gap and Arctic.
sections.whyItMatters: Nuclear policy is drifting from static posture toward active expansion across NATO's east. Lithuania's move, if completed, would be the most concrete change to the alliance's nuclear geography in years — and Russia is signaling it will treat any deployment as a targeting decision.

sections.heading: Ukraine: Russia's Jet-Drone Push and a Widening Budget Hole
sections.body:
Ukrainian intelligence has obtained internal Russian documents showing Moscow plans to spend $12 billion on jet-powered drones and loitering munitions next year, President Volodymyr Zelensky said. The Financial Times-adjacent reporting on jet drones notes the shift is already visible: jet-powered Geran variants flying at 400–650 km/h made up roughly half of Russia's nightly strike packages in early September, outrunning Ukraine's cheaper FPV interceptors. Kyiv has also been targeting a Russian weakness — Kyiv Post, citing Ukrainian military intelligence, reports disruption in Moscow's supply of Chinese-made jet engines for long-range strike drones.

But Ukraine's own finances are strained. Zelensky warned of 'serious challenges' with drones this winter, tying the problem to a $27 billion budget deficit heavily driven by defense production. On the export side, Ukraine's arms makers are still waiting to sell abroad despite fast-track approvals, according to reporting carried by Yahoo News.
sections.whyItMatters: Russia is industrializing a specific capability — cheap, fast, jet-propelled strike drones — faster than Ukraine can field matching interceptors. Kyiv's $27 billion deficit means the drone race is now as much a fiscal contest as a technological one.

bottomLine: Washington moved on two fronts to rebuild high-end air power: Boeing won the long-delayed F/A-XX carrier fighter, and Raytheon won a record $20.7 billion AMRAAM award designed to nearly double air-to-air missile output — the practical cost of the Iran war's expenditure. Both push more work through a shrinking US industrial base, and the AMRAAM deal is still unfunded by Congress. Elsewhere, Israel turned its wartime air-defense record into its largest export ever with Greece's €3 billion Achilles Shield, though the source-code dispute shows buyers cede real control; Japan opened its arms market in the biggest export-rule change in decades, potentially becoming a new Indo-Pacific supplier; and NATO's nuclear posture is hardening as Lithuania advances toward lifting its constitutional ban. The through-line: allies are buying capability faster than anyone is expanding the capacity to build it.
sources: Breaking Defense, The War Zone (TWZ), Anadolu Agency, Defense News, Reuters, AP, Politico Europe, defence-blog, Nordic Monitor (ORSAM), NHK, CSIS, Straits Times, Japan Today (Kyodo), EUobserver, The Defense Post, Izvestia, Euronews, Kyiv Post, Yahoo News, Financial Times, China Daily
